title: What's at the bottom of the ocean under the North Pole?

narration.heading: The North Pole
narration.text: You're standing on the North Pole. But under your boots, there's no ground at all.

narration.heading: Thin ice
narration.text: Just two to three metres of floating sea ice. Then you drop through into the Arctic Ocean.

narration.heading: Sunlight zone
narration.text: Two hundred metres down, the sunlight zone ends. Under the ice, it's already dim.

narration.heading: Nautilus
narration.text: In 1958, the submarine Nautilus passed right under this spot, the first to cross the Pole underwater.

narration.heading: 1,000 m down
narration.text: Past a thousand metres, no sunlight reaches at all. Total darkness, under total ice.

narration.heading: The long sink
narration.text: In 2007, two Russian submersibles, Mir One and Mir Two, took almost three hours to sink this far.

narration.heading: The seabed
narration.text: Four thousand two hundred and sixty-one metres: the seabed. They planted a titanium flag right here.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? There's no land at the North Pole. The nearest island is about seven hundred kilometres away.

narration.heading: Whose is it?
narration.text: Just drifting ice over four kilometres of ocean. So who do you think the North Pole belongs to?

skit.text: No land at the North Pole? So where does Santa park the sleigh?

titles: What if you sank to the seabed under the North Pole?
Sinking 4,261 m to the seabed under the North Pole
youtube.description: Drop through the sea ice at the North Pole and sink 4,261 metres to the seabed where a titanium flag was planted in 2007, and find out why there's no land at the Pole at all.

sources.claim: Sea ice at the North Pole is typically 2–3 m thick; the seabed is 4,261 m down (Mir, 2007); the nearest land, Kaffeklubben Island, is about 700 km away
USS Nautilus was the first submarine to complete a submerged transit of the North Pole, on 3 August 1958

On 2 August 2007, MIR-1 and MIR-2 reached the seabed at the Pole (MIR-1 at 4,261 m after about 2 h 40 min) and planted a titanium Russian flag; the expedition was tied to Russia's claim to the Lomonosov Ridge
The upper 200 m is the sunlight zone; below 1,000 m sunlight does not reach
